claim: Activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 cause severe short stature.
source: Activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor 3 and inactivating mutations in the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase both cause severe short stature, but how these two signaling systems interact to regulate bone growth is poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on FGFR3 mutations and achondroplasia.

claim: Inactivating mutations in the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase cause severe short stature.
source: Activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor 3 and inactivating mutations in the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase both cause severe short stature, but how these two signaling systems interact to regulate bone growth is poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on NPR2 mutations.

claim: Bone elongation is increased when NPR2 cannot be dephosphorylated.
source: Here, we show that bone elongation is increased when NPR2 cannot be dephosphorylated and thus produces more cyclic GMP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Npr2-7E mice showing longer bones.

claim: NPR2 that cannot be dephosphorylated produces more cyclic GMP.
source: Here, we show that bone elongation is increased when NPR2 cannot be dephosphorylated and thus produces more cyclic GMP.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of cGMP production in growth plates.

claim: FGF-induced dephosphorylation of NPR2 decreases its guanylyl cyclase activity in growth plate chondrocytes in living bone.
source: By developing an in vivo imaging system to measure cyclic GMP production in intact tibia, we show that FGF-induced dephosphorylation of NPR2 decreases its guanylyl cyclase activity in growth plate chondrocytes in living bone.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data showing reduced cGMP production after FGF treatment.

claim: The dephosphorylation of NPR2 requires a PPP-family phosphatase.
source: The dephosphorylation requires a PPP-family phosphatase.
evidence: Supported by experiments using cantharidin, a PPP-family phosphatase inhibitor.

claim: FGF signaling lowers cyclic GMP production in the growth plate.
source: Thus FGF signaling lowers cyclic GMP production in the growth plate, which counteracts bone elongation.
evidence: Supported by cGi500 imaging data showing reduced cGMP after FGF treatment.

claim: Lowering cyclic GMP production in the growth plate counteracts bone elongation.
source: Thus FGF signaling lowers cyclic GMP production in the growth plate, which counteracts bone elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of FGF effects on cGMP and known roles of cGMP in bone growth.

claim: Longitudinal growth of limbs and vertebrae depends on division and differentiation of chondrocytes within the cartilage growth plates.
source: Longitudinal growth of limbs and vertebrae depends on division and differentiation of chondrocytes within the cartilage growth plates located at each end of the growing bone (see Figure 2B), resulting in formation of a scaffold that is subsequently mineralized (Kozhemyakina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge in the field.

claim: NPR2 is found in growth plate chondrocytes.
source: One such regulator is the natriuretic peptide-stimulated guanylyl cyclase, natriuretic peptide receptor 2 (NPR2), also known as guanylyl cyclase B, which is found in growth plate chondrocytes and promotes bone elongation (Yasoda et al., 1998; Yamashita et al., 2000; Chusho et al., 2001; Tamura et al., 2004; Bartels et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPR2 promotes bone elongation.
source: One such regulator is the natriuretic peptide-stimulated guanylyl cyclase, natriuretic peptide receptor 2 (NPR2), also known as guanylyl cyclase B, which is found in growth plate chondrocytes and promotes bone elongation (Yasoda et al., 1998; Yamashita et al., 2000; Chusho et al., 2001; Tamura et al., 2004; Bartels et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inactivating mutations in NPR2 result in severe shortening of bones in mice and people, causing acromesomelic dysplasia type Maroteaux (AMDM).
source: Inactivating mutations in NPR2, which reduce cGMP, result in severe shortening of bones in mice and people, causing the condition acromesomelic dysplasia type Maroteaux (AMDM), in which height is reduced by ~30% (Maroteaux et al., 1971; Tamura et al., 2004; Bartels et al., 2004; Khan et al., 2012; Geister et al., 2013; Nakao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical and mouse studies.

claim: In AMDM, height is reduced by approximately 30%.
source: Inactivating mutations in NPR2, which reduce cGMP, result in severe shortening of bones in mice and people, causing the condition acromesomelic dysplasia type Maroteaux (AMDM), in which height is reduced by ~30% (Maroteaux et al., 1971; Tamura et al., 2004; Bartels et al., 2004; Khan et al., 2012; Geister et al., 2013; Nakao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Activating mutations of NPR2 result in longer bones.
source: Conversely, activating mutations of NPR2 result in longer bones (Miura et al., 2012; Hannema et al., 2013; Miura et al., 2014), opposite to what is seen with the AMDM patients.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase requires the extracellular binding of C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP).
source: Activation of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase requires the extracellular binding of C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) and also the phosphorylation of multiple intracellular juxtamembrane serines and threonines (Potter, 1998; Potter, 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Activation of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase requires the phosphorylation of multiple intracellular juxtamembrane serines and threonines.
source: Activation of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase requires the extracellular binding of C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) and also the phosphorylation of multiple intracellular juxtamembrane serines and threonines (Potter, 1998; Potter, 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: There is a close correlation between NPR2 phosphorylation and NPR2 activity.
source: Previous studies have established a close correlation between NPR2 phosphorylation and NPR2 activity (Abbey-Hosch et al., 2005; Egbert et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017), and if these phosphorylation sites are mutated to alanine, CNP-dependent guanylyl cyclase activity is reduced to only 6% of that of the wild type protein (Potter and Hunter, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If NPR2 phosphorylation sites are mutated to alanine, CNP-dependent guanylyl cyclase activity is reduced to only 6% of that of the wild type protein.
source: Previous studies have established a close correlation between NPR2 phosphorylation and NPR2 activity (Abbey-Hosch et al., 2005; Egbert et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2017), and if these phosphorylation sites are mutated to alanine, CNP-dependent guanylyl cyclase activity is reduced to only 6% of that of the wild type protein (Potter and Hunter, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: When the seven serines and threonines of NPR2 are mutated to glutamate (NPR2-7E), the maximal velocity of the CNP-dependent guanylyl cyclase activity is the same as that of the wild type enzyme.
source: Correspondingly, if the seven serines and threonines are mutated to the phosphomimetic amino acid glutamate (NPR2-7E), the maximal velocity of the CNP-dependent guanylyl cyclase activity is the same as that of the wild type enzyme, but does not decrease in response to stimuli that dephosphorylate and inactivate the wild type protein (Yoder et al., 2012; Shuhaibar et al., 2016; Robinson et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPR2-7E does not decrease in activity in response to stimuli that dephosphorylate and inactivate the wild type protein.
source: Correspondingly, if the seven serines and threonines are mutated to the phosphomimetic amino acid glutamate (NPR2-7E), the maximal velocity of the CNP-dependent guanylyl cyclase activity is the same as that of the wild type enzyme, but does not decrease in response to stimuli that dephosphorylate and inactivate the wild type protein (Yoder et al., 2012; Shuhaibar et al., 2016; Robinson et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dephosphorylation of NPR2 is a physiological mediator of hormonal signaling in ovarian follicles.
source: Our previous analysis of mice in which both copies of Npr2 were globally replaced with a sequence encoding NPR2-7E (Npr27E/7E) demonstrated that dephosphorylation of NPR2 is a physiological mediator of hormonal signaling in ovarian follicles (Shuhaibar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by the authors.

claim: Activating mutations of FGFR3 inhibit bone growth, causing achondroplasia.
source: Another essential regulator of bone elongation is FGF receptor 3 (FGFR3); activating mutations of FGFR3 inhibit bone growth, causing achondroplasia, in which human height is reduced by ~25% (Horton et al., 1978; Rousseau et al., 1994; Shiang et al., 1994; Naski et al., 1998; Wang et al., 1999; Lorget et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2017; Ornitz and Legeai-Mallet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical and research studies.

claim: In achondroplasia, human height is reduced by approximately 25%.
source: Another essential regulator of bone elongation is FGF receptor 3 (FGFR3); activating mutations of FGFR3 inhibit bone growth, causing achondroplasia, in which human height is reduced by ~25% (Horton et al., 1978; Rousseau et al., 1994; Shiang et al., 1994; Naski et al., 1998; Wang et al., 1999; Lorget et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2017; Ornitz and Legeai-Mallet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Mice and people lacking functional FGFR3 have longer bones.
source: Conversely, mice and people lacking functional FGFR3 have longer bones (Colvin et al., 1996; Deng et al., 1996; Makrythanasis et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of NPR2 by increasing CNP opposes the decrease in bone growth caused by activating mutations of FGFR3.
source: Intriguingly, the greatly reduced bone length seen with activating mutations of FGFR3, resembles that seen with inactivating mutations of NPR2, and activation of NPR2 by increasing CNP opposes the decrease in bone growth caused by activating mutations of FGFR3 (Yasoda et al., 2004; Yasoda et al., 2009; Lorget et al., 2012; Wendt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies of fibroblasts and chondrogenic cells have indicated that FGF signaling decreases NPR2 activity.
source: Furthermore, studies of fibroblasts and chondrogenic cells derived from embryonic carcinomas and chondrosarcomas have indicated that FGF signaling decreases NPR2 activity (Chrisman and Garbers, 1999; Ozasa et al., 2005; Robinson et al., 2017), and that the inactivation is due to dephosphorylation of NPR2 (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The inactivation of NPR2 by FGF is due to dephosphorylation of NPR2.
source: Furthermore, studies of fibroblasts and chondrogenic cells derived from embryonic carcinomas and chondrosarcomas have indicated that FGF signaling decreases NPR2 activity (Chrisman and Garbers, 1999; Ozasa et al., 2005; Robinson et al., 2017), and that the inactivation is due to dephosphorylation of NPR2 (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Npr27E/7E mice have longer tails than wild type mice.
source: Measurements at 8–16 weeks of age showed that the tails, femurs, tibias, and bodies of Npr27E/7E mice were 8% to 14% longer than wild type (Figure 1B,E,F,G; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Npr27E/7E mice have longer femurs than wild type mice.
source: Measurements at 8–16 weeks of age showed that the tails, femurs, tibias, and bodies of Npr27E/7E mice were 8% to 14% longer than wild type (Figure 1B,E,F,G; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Npr27E/7E mice have longer tibias than wild type mice.
source: Measurements at 8–16 weeks of age showed that the tails, femurs, tibias, and bodies of Npr27E/7E mice were 8% to 14% longer than wild type (Figure 1B,E,F,G; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Npr27E/7E mice have longer bodies than wild type mice.
source: Measurements at 8–16 weeks of age showed that the tails, femurs, tibias, and bodies of Npr27E/7E mice were 8% to 14% longer than wild type (Figure 1B,E,F,G; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Differences in limb and body length between Npr27E/7E and wild type mice were seen as early as 4 weeks.
source: Differences in limb and body length were seen as early as 4 weeks (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 1E-G.

claim: The fifth caudal vertebra was 18% longer in Npr27E/7E mice compared to wild type, as measured at 18 weeks.
source: The fifth caudal vertebra was 18% longer, as measured at 18 weeks (Figure 1C,D; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: When NPR2 cannot be inactivated by dephosphorylation, endochondral bone growth is increased.
source: These results indicate that when NPR2 cannot be inactivated by dephosphorylation, endochondral bone growth is increased.
evidence: Inferred from the bone length measurements in Npr27E/7E mice.

claim: The width of the cranium is unaffected in Npr27E/7E mice.
source: The width of the cranium, which is dependent on membranous, not endochondral, bone growth was unaffected (Figure 1H; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The increases in body and bone length in Npr27E/7E mice phenocopied those previously reported for mice in which NPR2 activity was increased by overexpression of CNP or by an activating mutation in the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase domain.
source: The increases in body and bone length, which resulted from an inability of NPR2 to be inactivated by dephosphorylation, phenocopied those previously reported for mice in which NPR2 activity was increased by overexpression of the NPR2 agonist CNP or by an activating mutation in the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase domain (Yasoda et al., 2004; Miura et al., 2012) and in a human patient with the same activating mutation in NPR2, who was 14% taller than average at 15 years of age (Miura et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A human patient with an activating mutation in NPR2 was 14% taller than average at 15 years of age.
source: The increases in body and bone length, which resulted from an inability of NPR2 to be inactivated by dephosphorylation, phenocopied those previously reported for mice in which NPR2 activity was increased by overexpression of the NPR2 agonist CNP or by an activating mutation in the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase domain (Yasoda et al., 2004; Miura et al., 2012) and in a human patient with the same activating mutation in NPR2, who was 14% taller than average at 15 years of age (Miura et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: NPR2 is expressed in tissues outside of the bone growth plate, including the pituitary and gastro-intestinal tract.
source: Because NPR2 is expressed in tissues outside of the bone growth plate, including the pituitary and gastro-intestinal tract (Tamura and Garbers, 2003; Sogawa et al., 2010), we tested whether the longer bones of the Npr27E/7E mice resulted from a direct action on bone rather than an indirect action on other tissues.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When first dissected, Npr27E/7E and wild type tibia did not differ in length.
source: When first dissected, Npr27E/7E and wild type tibia did not differ in length (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No difference in body or tibia length is seen at birth comparing mice with inactivated NPR2 and wild type mice.
source: The absence of a detectable difference in length is consistent with previous studies showing no difference in body or tibia length at birth comparing mice with inactivated NPR2 and wild type mice (Tamura et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Little or no difference in body or bone length is seen at birth of humans with inactivating NPR2 mutations.
source: Likewise, little or no difference in body or bone length is seen at birth of humans with inactivating NPR2 mutations (Bartels et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: NPR2 activity is not required for prenatal bone elongation.
source: These previous studies indicate that NPR2 activity is not required for prenatal bone elongation.
evidence: Inferred from cited studies showing no difference in bone length at birth.

claim: When bones of newborn mice were placed in culture, the rate of bone elongation over a 6 day period was reduced if the Npr2 gene was disrupted.
source: However, when bones of newborn mice were placed in culture, the rate of bone elongation over a 6 day period was reduced if the Npr2 gene was disrupted (Tamura et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: When cultured in the presence of 1 μM CNP and measured over a period of 6 days, the rate of bone elongation was greater for Npr27E/7E compared with wild type tibia.
source: Correspondingly, when cultured in the presence of 1 μM CNP and measured over a period of 6 days, the rate of bone elongation was greater for Npr27E/7E compared with wild type tibia (Figure 2A,D; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: For the proximal epiphysis, there was a 14% greater elongation rate for Npr27E/7E compared to wild type.
source: For the proximal epiphysis, there was a 14% greater elongation rate for Npr27E/7E compared to wild type (Figure 2E; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Npr27E/7E mice have longer bones due to a direct effect of the mutations on NPR2 function within the bone itself.
source: These results show that Npr27E/7E mice have longer bones due to a direct effect of the mutations on NPR2 function within the bone itself.
evidence: Inferred from cultured bone experiments showing increased growth rate.

claim: There was no effect of the Npr27E/7E mutations on bone elongation in medium without added CNP.
source: Interestingly, there was no effect of the Npr27E/7E mutations on bone elongation in medium without added CNP (Figure 2F,G; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: CNP produced by the bones of 3–10 day old mice is not sufficient to activate NPR2 under the culture conditions used.
source: This result suggests CNP produced by the bones of 3–10 day old mice is not sufficient to activate NPR2, at least under our culture conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of difference in bone elongation without added CNP.

claim: NPR2 activity has been previously measured using homogenates of fetal tibia.
source: NPR2 activity has been previously measured using homogenates of fetal tibia (Yasoda et al., 1998) and membrane preparations from chondrocyte cell lines (Ozasa et al., 2005; Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPR2 activity has been previously measured using membrane preparations from chondrocyte cell lines.
source: NPR2 activity has been previously measured using homogenates of fetal tibia (Yasoda et al., 1998) and membrane preparations from chondrocyte cell lines (Ozasa et al., 2005; Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: cGi500 is comprised of cyan fluorescent protein (CFP) and yellow fluorescent protein (YFP), linked by a cGMP-binding domain.
source: cGi500 is comprised of cyan fluorescent protein (CFP) and yellow fluorescent protein (YFP), linked by a cGMP-binding domain; the sensitivity of cGi500 to cGMP is based on Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the cGi500 sensor design.

claim: The sensitivity of cGi500 to cGMP is based on Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET).
source: cGi500 is comprised of cyan fluorescent protein (CFP) and yellow fluorescent protein (YFP), linked by a cGMP-binding domain; the sensitivity of cGi500 to cGMP is based on Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of FRET-based sensors.

claim: Binding of cGMP to the linker domain of cGi500 causes the CFP and YFP domains to move farther apart.
source: Binding of cGMP to the linker domain causes the CFP and YFP domains to move farther apart.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cGi500 sensor mechanism.

claim: The CFP/YFP emission ratio is higher when the cGMP concentration is higher.
source: Thus measurement of the relative intensities of the light emitted by CFP and YFP provides an indicator of the cGMP concentration. The CFP/YFP emission ratio is higher when the cGMP concentration is higher, with a half-maximal response at 500 nM cGMP, and a dynamic range of ~100 nM to ~3 μM cGMP (Russwurm et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization of the sensor.

claim: cGi500 has a half-maximal response at 500 nM cGMP.
source: Thus measurement of the relative intensities of the light emitted by CFP and YFP provides an indicator of the cGMP concentration. The CFP/YFP emission ratio is higher when the cGMP concentration is higher, with a half-maximal response at 500 nM cGMP, and a dynamic range of ~100 nM to ~3 μM cGMP (Russwurm et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization of the sensor.

claim: cGi500 has a dynamic range of approximately 100 nM to approximately 3 μM cGMP.
source: Thus measurement of the relative intensities of the light emitted by CFP and YFP provides an indicator of the cGMP concentration. The CFP/YFP emission ratio is higher when the cGMP concentration is higher, with a half-maximal response at 500 nM cGMP, and a dynamic range of ~100 nM to ~3 μM cGMP (Russwurm et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization of the sensor.

claim: Excitation of CFP resulted in fluorescence in all regions of the growth plate.
source: Excitation of CFP resulted in fluorescence in all regions of the growth plate (Figure 3D), allowing identification of chondrocytes at different stages of development, based on the shape of the cells: round (also called resting), columnar (also called proliferating), and hypertrophic (Kozhemyakina et al., 2015; Ornitz and Legeai-Mallet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Columnar/prehypertrophic cells express both NPR2 and FGFR3.
source: Columnar cells that are beginning to increase their volume, referred to as 'prehypertrophic', express both NPR2 and FGFR3 (Yamashita et al., 2000; Chusho et al., 2001; de Frutos et al., 2007; Kozhemyakina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In response to CNP, the CFP emission intensity increased and the YFP emission intensity decreased.
source: In response to CNP, the CFP emission intensity increased and the YFP emission intensity decreased (Figure 3F), resulting in a higher CFP/YFP ratio (Figure 3G) and indicating an increase in cGMP due to activation of NPR2.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CNP perfusion resulted in a higher CFP/YFP ratio, indicating an increase in cGMP due to activation of NPR2.
source: In response to CNP, the CFP emission intensity increased and the YFP emission intensity decreased (Figure 3F), resulting in a higher CFP/YFP ratio (Figure 3G) and indicating an increase in cGMP due to activation of NPR2.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Confocal microscopy of isolated tibia expressing cGi500 allowed monitoring of NPR2 activity in the live and intact growth plate for the first time.
source: Thus, confocal microscopy of isolated tibia expressing cGi500 allowed us to monitor NPR2 activity in the live and intact growth plate for the first time.
evidence: Based on the novelty of the developed method.

claim: FGF18 is one of the two redundant FGF isoforms that function to activate FGFR3 in the growth plate.
source: Among the many FGF isoforms, we used FGF18 because it is one of the two redundant FGF isoforms that function to activate FGFR3 in the growth plate (Ornitz and Marie, 2015; Hung et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In tibias without FGF18 pretreatment, perfusion of CNP caused a large increase in the concentration of cGMP.
source: In tibias without FGF18 pretreatment, perfusion of CNP through the imaging chamber caused a large increase in the concentration of cGMP (Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: If the tibias were pretreated with FGF18, the CNP-induced increase in cGMP was smaller.
source: However, if the tibias were pretreated with FGF18, the CNP-induced increase in cGMP was smaller (Figure 4A,G; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A,G.

claim: In chondrocytes within a living growth plate, FGF signaling reduces the activity of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase.
source: These results indicate that in chondrocytes within a living growth plate, FGF signaling reduces the activity of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced cGMP production after FGF treatment.

claim: The baseline CFP/YFP ratio before CNP perfusion was the same with and without FGF pretreatment.
source: The baseline CFP/YFP ratio before CNP perfusion was the same with and without FGF pretreatment, suggesting that FGF had no effect on the baseline cGMP concentration (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Before CNP treatment, the cGMP content of the epiphysis was only 1–2% of that after CNP addition.
source: Before CNP treatment, the cGMP content of the epiphysis was only 1–2% of that after CNP addition (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1), and no significant effect of an 80 min preincubation with FGF was detected (Figure 5B; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant effect of an 80 min preincubation with FGF on baseline cGMP content was detected.
source: Before CNP treatment, the cGMP content of the epiphysis was only 1–2% of that after CNP addition (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1), and no significant effect of an 80 min preincubation with FGF was detected (Figure 5B; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In growth plates assayed after CNP addition, FGF pretreatment for 80 min decreased cGMP content to 40% of the initial level.
source: These cGMP ELISA measurements also showed that in growth plates assayed after CNP addition, FGF pretreatment for 80 min decreased cGMP content to 40% of the initial level (Figure 5A), consistent with the cGi500 measurements.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Studies of the RCS chondrocyte cell line have shown that FGF signaling decreases NPR2 phosphorylation and activity.
source: Studies of the RCS chondrocyte cell line have shown that FGF signaling decreases NPR2 phosphorylation and activity, and that the decrease in activity depends on the decrease in phosphorylation (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The decrease in NPR2 activity in response to FGF depends on the decrease in phosphorylation.
source: Studies of the RCS chondrocyte cell line have shown that FGF signaling decreases NPR2 phosphorylation and activity, and that the decrease in activity depends on the decrease in phosphorylation (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Growth plates from Npr27E/7E mice showed an increase in cGMP when exposed to CNP.
source: As with wild type, growth plates from Npr27E/7E mice showed an increase in cGMP when exposed to CNP (Figure 4D; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The CNP-stimulated cGMP increase was greater for Npr27E/7E vs wild type.
source: In fact, the CNP-stimulated cGMP increase was greater for Npr27E/7E vs wild type (Figure 4G; Figure 4—source data 1), as would be expected if NPR2 in the wild type growth plate was partially dephosphorylated as a result of signaling by endogenous hormones or growth factors (compare diagrams in Figure 4B and E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The higher NPR2 activity measured in the Npr27E/7E vs wild type growth plate was not explained by a difference in the amount of NPR2 protein.
source: The higher NPR2 activity measured in the Npr27E/7E vs wild type growth plate was not explained by a difference in the amount of NPR2 protein, which was similar for the growth plate region of the two genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 7E enzyme has a somewhat lower Km for GTP than the wildtype enzyme.
source: Another possible explanation of the higher NPR2 activity observed for the Npr27E/7E genotype compared to wild type is that the 7E enzyme has a somewhat lower Km for GTP than the wildtype enzyme, although at the GTP concentrations found in most intact tissues (Traut, 1994), the difference in enzyme activity would be small.
evidence: Based on known biochemical properties of the enzyme.

claim: The 7E mutations have no effect on the CNP concentration required to activate NPR2 to half its maximum value.
source: The 7E mutations also have no effect on the CNP concentration required to activate NPR2 to half its maximum value (Shuhaibar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In growth plates from Npr27E/7E mice, FGF pretreatment did not cause a decrease in CNP-stimulated cGMP production.
source: Importantly, in growth plates from Npr27E/7E mice, FGF pretreatment did not cause a decrease in CNP-stimulated cGMP production (Figure 4D,G).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D,G.

claim: Because the NPR2-7E protein cannot be dephosphorylated, FGF signaling does not reduce its enzyme activity.
source: This lack of response to FGF contrasts with the FGF-induced decrease in NPR2 activity that is seen with wild type (Figure 4A,G), and indicates that because the NPR2-7E protein cannot be dephosphorylated, FGF signaling does not reduce its enzyme activity (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of FGF effect on Npr27E/7E growth plates.

claim: FGF signaling reduces cGMP production by dephosphorylating NPR2 in the growth plate.
source: These results support the conclusion that FGF signaling reduces cGMP production by dephosphorylating NPR2 in the growth plate.
evidence: Inferred from the differential response of wild type vs Npr27E/7E to FGF.

claim: A PPP-family phosphatase mediates the dephosphorylation of NPR2 in response to luteinizing hormone in ovarian follicles.
source: Our previous studies of NPR2 activity in ovarian follicles indicated that a PPP-family phosphatase mediates the dephosphorylation of NPR2 in response to luteinizing hormone (Egbert et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by the authors.

claim: At 100 μM, cantharidin selectively inhibits the PPP family phosphatases, PPP1, PPP2, PPP4, and PPP5.
source: At 100 μM, cantharidin selectively inhibits the PPP family phosphatases, PPP1, PPP2 (also known as PP2A), PPP4, and PPP5 (Swingle et al., 2007; Pereira et al., 2011) but does not inhibit PPP3 (also known as PP2B or calcineurin) (Honkanen, 1993; Pereira et al., 2011) or PPM (also known as PP2C) (Li et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on cantharidin specificity.

claim: Cantharidin does not inhibit PPP3 (also known as PP2B or calcineurin).
source: At 100 μM, cantharidin selectively inhibits the PPP family phosphatases, PPP1, PPP2 (also known as PP2A), PPP4, and PPP5 (Swingle et al., 2007; Pereira et al., 2011) but does not inhibit PPP3 (also known as PP2B or calcineurin) (Honkanen, 1993; Pereira et al., 2011) or PPM (also known as PP2C) (Li et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on cantharidin specificity.

claim: Cantharidin does not inhibit PPM (also known as PP2C).
source: At 100 μM, cantharidin selectively inhibits the PPP family phosphatases, PPP1, PPP2 (also known as PP2A), PPP4, and PPP5 (Swingle et al., 2007; Pereira et al., 2011) but does not inhibit PPP3 (also known as PP2B or calcineurin) (Honkanen, 1993; Pereira et al., 2011) or PPM (also known as PP2C) (Li et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on cantharidin specificity.

claim: Control tibias without cantharidin treatment showed the expected decrease in CNP-dependent cGMP production in response to FGF-18.
source: Control tibias without cantharidin treatment showed the expected decrease in CNP-dependent cGMP production in response to FGF-18 (Figure 6A,C; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Tibias that had been pre-incubated with cantharidin showed no difference in NPR2 activity comparing those that had or had not been treated with FGF-18.
source: However, tibias that had been pre-incubated with cantharidin showed no difference in NPR2 activity comparing those that had or had not been treated with FGF-18 (Figure 6B,C; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Like the Npr27E/7E mutation, cantharidin inhibits the decrease in cGMP production in response to FGF.
source: These results show that like the Npr27E/7E mutation, cantharidin inhibits the decrease in cGMP production in response to FGF.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of FGF effect in cantharidin-treated tibias.

claim: Preventing the dephosphorylation of NPR2 prevents the decrease in NPR2 activity in response to FGF.
source: These experiments provide independent evidence that preventing the dephosphorylation of NPR2 prevents the decrease in NPR2 activity, and also indicate that a PPP family phosphatase is responsible for the dephosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from cantharidin experiments.

claim: A PPP family phosphatase is responsible for the dephosphorylation of NPR2 in response to FGF.
source: These experiments provide independent evidence that preventing the dephosphorylation of NPR2 prevents the decrease in NPR2 activity, and also indicate that a PPP family phosphatase is responsible for the dephosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from cantharidin experiments showing inhibition of FGF effect.

claim: Phosphorylation of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase promotes bone elongation.
source: Our findings identify two new components of the signaling network by which FGFR3 and NPR2 signaling regulate bone growth. Firstly, our results indicate that phosphorylation of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase promotes bone elongation; this conclusion is based on our finding that a mutation that prevents NPR2 dephosphorylation results in longer bones.
evidence: Inferred from the longer bones in Npr27E/7E mice.

claim: Part of the mechanism by which FGF signaling inhibits bone elongation is by decreasing NPR2 phosphorylation and activity.
source: Secondly, our results indicate that part of the mechanism by which FGF signaling inhibits bone elongation is by decreasing NPR2 phosphorylation and activity.
evidence: Inferred from the FGF effects on cGMP production and the lack of effect in Npr27E/7E mice.

claim: Mice lacking the FGFR3 receptor show a greater increase in bone length (approximately 7–40%) than mice with the mutation that prevents dephosphorylation of NPR2 (8–14%).
source: However, mice lacking the FGFR3 receptor (Colvin et al., 1996; Deng et al., 1996) show a greater increase in bone length (~7–40%) than we report here for mice with the mutation that prevents dephosphorylation of NPR2 (8–14%), consistent with previous studies identifying multiple mechanisms by which FGF signaling opposes bone elongation (Ornitz and Legeai-Mallet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and comparison with current data.

claim: FGF signaling opposes bone elongation through multiple mechanisms.
source: However, mice lacking the FGFR3 receptor (Colvin et al., 1996; Deng et al., 1996) show a greater increase in bone length (~7–40%) than we report here for mice with the mutation that prevents dephosphorylation of NPR2 (8–14%), consistent with previous studies identifying multiple mechanisms by which FGF signaling opposes bone elongation (Ornitz and Legeai-Mallet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: An important pathway by which FGFR3 signaling decreases bone elongation is by activation of MAP kinase.
source: An important pathway by which FGFR3 signaling decreases bone elongation is by activation of MAP kinase (see Ornitz and Legeai-Mallet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: An important pathway by which NPR2 guanylyl cyclase activity increases bone elongation is by elevating cGMP and activating the cGMP-dependent protein kinase PRKG2.
source: An important pathway by which NPR2 guanylyl cyclase activity increases bone elongation is by elevating cGMP and activating the cGMP-dependent protein kinase PRKG2 (Pfeifer et al., 1996; Chikuda et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Application of CNP to increase NPR2 guanylyl cyclase activity in chondrocytes inhibits FGF-induced MAP kinase activation.
source: Previous studies have established that application of CNP to increase NPR2 guanylyl cyclase activity in chondrocytes, thus elevating cGMP and stimulating cGMP-dependent protein kinase, inhibits FGF-induced MAP kinase activation (Yasoda et al., 2004; Krejci et al., 2005; Ozasa et al., 2005; Kamemura et al., 2017), which would counteract FGF-inhibition of bone growth (solid blue line in Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Inhibition of FGF-induced MAP kinase activation by cGMP-dependent protein kinase would counteract FGF-inhibition of bone growth.
source: Previous studies have established that application of CNP to increase NPR2 guanylyl cyclase activity in chondrocytes, thus elevating cGMP and stimulating cGMP-dependent protein kinase, inhibits FGF-induced MAP kinase activation (Yasoda et al., 2004; Krejci et al., 2005; Ozasa et al., 2005; Kamemura et al., 2017), which would counteract FGF-inhibition of bone growth (solid blue line in Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from the known effects of MAP kinase on bone growth.

claim: FGF activation of FGFR3 acts by way of a PPP family phosphatase to decrease the phosphorylation and activity of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase.
source: Our findings indicate that FGF activation of its receptor FGFR3 acts by way of a PPP family phosphatase to decrease the phosphorylation and activity of the NPR2 guanylyl cyclase, thus reducing production of cGMP.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data with FGF, Npr27E/7E mice, and cantharidin.

claim: Cyclic GMP increases bone growth by activating the cGMP-dependent protein kinase PRKG2.
source: Cyclic GMP increases bone growth by activating the cGMP-dependent protein kinase PRKG2.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FGF signaling could cause dephosphorylation of NPR2 by inactivation of the kinase(s) that phosphorylate NPR2.
source: How FGF signaling causes dephosphorylation of NPR2 remains to be determined; this could occur by inactivation of the kinase(s) that phosphorylate NPR2, and/or by activation of the phosphatase(s) that dephosphorylate it.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: FGF signaling could cause dephosphorylation of NPR2 by activation of the phosphatase(s) that dephosphorylate it.
source: How FGF signaling causes dephosphorylation of NPR2 remains to be determined; this could occur by inactivation of the kinase(s) that phosphorylate NPR2, and/or by activation of the phosphatase(s) that dephosphorylate it.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: PPP2 is activated by FGF signaling in the RCS chondrocyte cell line.
source: Activation of PPP2 is one possibility, since PPP2 is activated by FGF signaling in the RCS chondrocyte cell line (Kolupaeva et al., 2013), and purified PPP2 can dephosphorylate NPR2 in vitro (Potter, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Purified PPP2 can dephosphorylate NPR2 in vitro.
source: Activation of PPP2 is one possibility, since PPP2 is activated by FGF signaling in the RCS chondrocyte cell line (Kolupaeva et al., 2013), and purified PPP2 can dephosphorylate NPR2 in vitro (Potter, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In patients with achondroplasia, stimulation of NPR2 by subcutaneous injection of a hydrolysis-resistant analog of CNP increases bone length.
source: Ongoing clinical trials have shown that in patients with achondroplasia, in which skeletal dysplasia is caused by a constitutively active form of FGFR3, stimulation of NPR2 by subcutaneous injection of a hydrolysis-resistant analog of CNP increases bone length (Klag and Horton, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical trial report.

claim: Increasing CNP in mouse models of achondroplasia increases bone growth.
source: These results are consistent with the increased bone growth that results from increasing CNP in mouse models of achondroplasia (Yasoda et al., 2004; Yasoda et al., 2009; Lorget et al., 2012; Wendt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In a mouse model overexpressing a constitutively active form of FGFR3, applying CNP or a CNP analog in vivo or in vitro completely rescued the growth defect.
source: Studies using a mouse model overexpressing a constitutively active form of FGFR3 showed that applying CNP or a CNP analog in vivo or in vitro completely rescued the growth defect (Yasoda et al., 2004; Yasoda et al., 2009; Wendt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mice in which one allele of the Fgfr3 gene was replaced with a constitutively active form, treatment with the CNP analog increased the growth rate of cultured tibia only partially, from approximately 40% to approximately 70% of wild type.
source: However, in a study involving mice in which one allele of the Fgfr3 gene was replaced with a constitutively active form, as occurs in achondroplasia, it was found that treatment with the CNP analog increased the growth rate of cultured tibia only partially, from ~40% to~70% of wild type (Lorget et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: NPR2 guanylyl cyclase activity depends on the presence of CNP and on phosphorylation of multiple regulatory serines and threonines of NPR2.
source: Such incomplete rescue might be expected, considering that NPR2 guanylyl cyclase activity depends not only on the presence of CNP but also on phosphorylation of multiple regulatory serines and threonines of NPR2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NPR2 regulation.

claim: CNP levels are elevated in patients with achondroplasia.
source: CNP levels are elevated in patients with achondroplasia, suggesting that NPR2 in their chondrocytes is resistant to CNP (Olney et al., 2015), which could be due to NPR2 dephosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: NPR2 in chondrocytes of achondroplasia patients may be resistant to CNP, which could be due to NPR2 dephosphorylation.
source: CNP levels are elevated in patients with achondroplasia, suggesting that NPR2 in their chondrocytes is resistant to CNP (Olney et al., 2015), which could be due to NPR2 dephosphorylation.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on elevated CNP levels and known effects of dephosphorylation.

claim: If NPR2 phosphorylation could be increased in chondrocytes of achondroplasia patients by inhibiting the phosphatase that dephosphorylates NPR2, this could potentially enhance the therapeutic stimulation of NPR2 activity by CNP.
source: Thus, if NPR2 phosphorylation could be increased in chondrocytes of these patients, by inhibiting the phosphatase that dephosphorylates NPR2, this could potentially enhance the therapeutic stimulation of NPR2 activity by CNP as a treatment for achondroplasia.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic approach.

claim: Findings with the phosphatase inhibitor cantharidin support the concept of using related phosphatase inhibitors for treatment of achondroplasia.
source: Our findings with the phosphatase inhibitor cantharidin support the concept of using related phosphatase inhibitors (Lu et al., 2009; Chung et al., 2017) for treatment of achondroplasia.
evidence: Inferred from the cantharidin experiments and cited related compounds.
